Salford City Council - Record of Decision
Affordable Housing
Development - A2 Robert Hall Street, Ordsall
 
I Councillor Mike McCusker, Deputy City Mayor and Lead
Member for Planning, Transport, Sustainable Development and
Regeneration, in exercise of the powers contained within the City
Council Constitution, and
following consultation with Cabinet, do hereby approve:
 
1. Approve the funding mix for the scheme as detailed in the
report including the
    proposed capital expenditure within
the Housing Strategy Capital Programme.
 
2. Approve entering into a
Grant Funding agreement with the Greater Manchester
    Combined Authority (GMCA) for Good
Growth Funding support.
 
3. Approve The Council
obtaining grant funding from Homes England under its
   Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP)
on the basis detailed in the
   accompanying report.
 
4. Delegate authority to the
Executive Director of Place in consultation with the
    S151 officer to: negotiate, agree, and
finalise the detailed terms of the
 
  transaction and funding
agreements, including any required variations to the
    currently proposed funding
mix.
 
5. 
Authorise the Shared Legal Service, or externally appointed
solicitors, to
     prepare all necessary
documentation and to take all steps which are required
to
     give effect to the above
recommendations.
 
6.  That the
decision of the Procurement Board of 14th September 2026
approving
    
the appointment of Seddon Construction (which is subject to and
conditional on
    
confirmation of grant funding from Homes England and the GMCA), be
noted.
 
The Reasons are approval will enable the Council to finalise funding
arrangements, progress the construction contract and commence
delivery of the scheme in accordance with the programme, supporting
the Council's commitment to increasing the supply of affordable
homes and creating sustainable communities across Salford.
All procedures are in accordance with standing
orders. 
 
Options considered and rejected were: None. 
 
Assessment of Risk:
Medium - should this project not proceed it
will significantly impact the next phases of affordable housing for
the city, a key priority.

Salford City Council - Record of Decision
 
I, Councillor Mike McCusker, Deputy City Mayor and Lead
Member for Planning, Transport, Sustainable Development and
Regeneration , in exercise of the powers contained within the City
Council Constitution do hereby
approve the write off
of debt relating to Kiki Concepts Limited (Menagerie) following
them entering administration.
 
The Reasons are:
The Council has exhausted all legal avenues to
recover the debt. From an accounting perspective, the adjustment
ensures accurate financial reporting, while from an estate
management standpoint, it enables the release of funds to reimburse
outstanding service charges. The current debt position has created
cashflow constraints for the building’s managing agents,
delaying payments to suppliers, many of whom are local businesses,
thereby impacting the wider supply chain. Resolving this matter
promptly will restore financial stability and support ongoing
estate operations.
 
Options considered and rejected were: 
As noted above, there are no viable recovery
options available. The former tenant entered into administration, a
statutory moratorium came into effect which has prevented the
Council from taking steps to recover the outstanding debt. As such,
the only appropriate course of action is to write off the
outstanding amount in accordance with the Council's financial
procedures.
 
Assessment of Risk: Low
 
The source of funding is: N/A
 
Legal Advice obtained: External Legal Advisors 
As the Debt fell due before the Administrators
were appointed, this sum, like the Payment, will rank as an
unsecured claim in the Administration.
Moreover, and considering the moratorium on
enforcement action, the options open to SCC to recover this sum are
very limited and there is no guarantor of the Lease that SCC could
enforce against in this regard.
On that basis, and assuming KCL did not want
to assign the Lease in due course, we consider the likelihood of
SCC being able to recover the Debt from KCL to be unlikely.
 
 
Financial Advice obtained: Rafeeah Khan, Senior Accountant
This
report seeks approval for the write-off of debt relating to Kiki
Concepts Limited (Menagerie) following Administration. Ground Floor
Unit 2 was let to Kiki Concepts Ltd on a lease from 4th August 2016
to 28th April 2041, with no break until April 2031.
 
The total arrears proposed for write-off
amount to £637,455.98 (gross) comprising:
 
Rent:                         
£289,798.64
Utilities:                     
£318,528.86
Service
charge:       
£27,595.20
Insurance:                
£1,533.28
 
These debts were incurred prior to the
appointment of administrators on 7th November 2024 and rank as
unsecured claims in the administration process. Given the statutory
moratorium on enforcement action and the absence of a guarantor,
recovery options are extremely limited. The latest
administrator’s report (May 2025) confirmed that no dividend
is expected for unsecured creditors, and the company will likely
move to dissolution.
 
Financial Implications of the proposed debt
write-off for the Council as the principal landlord are:
VAT applies to all taxable supplies (rent,
service charges, utilities, and insurance)  under the lease. Following the tenant’s
administration and approval of the report recommendation, the
invoices will be credited, and the VAT originally charged becomes
irrecoverable because the supply is effectively cancelled, as the
HMRC requires credit notes to reverse VAT in these circumstances.
After crediting, costs such as service charges, utilities, and
insurance will fall to the Council as void costs, as they relate to
maintaining the property for future lettings. These costs will be
recharged internally on a net basis without VAT, as there is no
onward taxable supply to the insolvent tenant.
The financial impact is therefore two-fold:
the Council will absorb £289,714.45 of void costs (net
service charges, utilities, and insurance) while also losing rental
income of £241,498.87, which affects commercial income
targets but does not create a direct cash outflow. This treatment
ensures compliance with VAT regulations and accurately reflects the
cost of insolvency to the Council.
The proposed write-off will be funded from the
New Bailey Reserve. The New Bailey Reserve was established to
provide financial resilience for the estate, covering unforeseen
costs and mitigating risks associated with tenant defaults to
ensure operational stability. It also acts as a buffer against
market volatility and safeguards cashflow. The anticipated drawdown
from the reserve has already been reflected within the revenue
budget monitoring position.
 
It should also be noted, that the Council
remains liable for its headlease with its superior landlord.

The source of funding and

The
proposed 16-month direct award to Riverside (SASH), at a cost of
£374,453.33, represents a substantial increase compared with
the previous annual contract value of £75,122. This increase
reflects both the growing complexity of clients accessing the
service and the requirement to provide a 24-hour support
offer.
 
The
total contract value of £374,453.33 creates a significant
budget pressure. Funding for the award will be met through approved
Housing and Homelessness budgets for 2026/27 and 2027/28, with
additional GMCA funding secured for the same period. These funding
arrangements will support delivery of the service throughout the
proposed contract term. Any ongoing financial commitment and
associated budget pressure beyond 2027/28 will be considered
through the Council's Medium Term Financial Plan from 2028/29
onwards.
 
Despite the increase in contract value, the proposed uplift
reflects a combination of increased staffing requirements to
support a more complex client cohort, inflationary pressures and
the need to maintain safe 24-hour service delivery. The high-level
benchmarking undertaken indicates the scheme continues to represent
good value for money when assessed on a unit cost basis and against
alternative provision.
 
The
proposed increase cannot be accommodated within the existing
contract due to procurement regulations. As such, a 16-month direct
award under the Procurement Act 2023 is proposed to ensure
continuity of service provision.
 
This
approach represents a short-term solution, allowing time to review
future service delivery and commissioning options. Any ongoing cost
pressures will need to be considered as part of future financial
planning.
 
Legal Advice obtained:
Kathryn Saldanha, Commercial Team, Shared Legal Service
06/07/26
The
council’s current contract with The Riverside Group
(Riverside) was procured in 2021 under the Public Contracts
Regulations 2015 (PCR) and the council’s Constitution and
Contract Standing Orders (CSOs). Regulation 72 of the PCR sets out
the circumstances under which modifications to public contracts can
be made without conducting a new procurement procedure. The
proposed increase in the value of the contract for the period from
1 December 2026 to 31 March 2028 means that it is not possible for
the council to modify its current contract under Regulation 72 of
the PCR. As set out in the main body of this report, the multiple
and complex needs of the Clients who receive accommodation and
support services from Riverside means that there is a shortage of
providers who are able to provide schemes with the required wrap
around 24-hour support.
 
The
Procurement Act 2023 (PA) and the council’s Constitution and
CSOs allow the council to make a direct award of a contract without
a competitive tendering procedure under certain circumstances.
Under the PA, a transparency notice must be published by the
council before a contract is directly awarded. The function of the
transparency notice is to inform stakeholders that the council
intends to directly award a contract and ensure that there is
transparency relating to this decision. It provides an opportunity
for interested parties to consider the justification for direct
award. Schedule 5 of the PA sets out the “Direct Award
Justifications” which allow the council to make a direct
award of a contract under Section 41 of the PA. In the case of the
council’s direct award of this contract to The Riverside
Group for the period from 1 December 2026 to 31 March 2028, the
council believes that the “urgency” Direct Award
Justification at Schedule 5, Paragraphs 13 and 14 of the PA applies
and that:
 

(a)       the goods, services
or works to be supplied under the public contract are strictly
necessary for reasons of extreme and unavoidable urgency,
and

(b)       as a result the
public contract cannot be awarded on the basis of a competitive
tendering procedure.
 
The
council believes that the urgency for the direct award of this
contract to The Riverside Group is “unavoidable” as in
the urgency “is not attributable to any act or omission
of” the council, and “could not have been
foreseen” by the council.
 
Rule
9.13 of the council’s CSOs deals with “Exceptions to
Competition/Contractual Standing Orders” and allows for
exceptions to be made in the following circumstances:
 
•
Special education, health or social care contracts, if, it is
considered in the Council’s interests and to meet its
obligations under relevant legislation.
 
• The
execution of works or the supply of goods and services that are
required so urgently as not to permit compliance with the
requirements of competition.
 
As
set out in the main body of this report, the council is only
proposing to make a direct award of this contract to The Riverside
Group for a 16-month period which will give the council the
opportunity to review alternative long-term solutions.
 
As set out at
paragraph 3.0 of the report, at the time that the Council’s
current contract with The Riverside Group was awarded there was no
requirement for social value targets. The Council has worked with
The Riverside Group to identify a range of social value Themes,
Outcomes & Measures (TOMS) for the proposed new 16-month
contract which will be monitored and recorded by the Council
through formal contract meetings with The Riverside Group, rather
than through The Social Value Portal.

appropriate to extend the agreement on the same terms or to rely on
the existing framework provisions with an alternative provider. In

required to set out and justify the rationale for a direct award.
Following this approach will ensure that the contract remains
compliant with the requirements of the Procurement Act 2023 and the
Council’s internal governance processes.

The
proposed two?year extension of the Abbott Lodge contract, at a cost
of £288,451.96, is affordable within existing approved
Housing and Homelessness revenue budgets and represents good value
for money at this time. Although the benchmarking undertaken is
high level, it indicates that the service provides 24?hour
complex?needs support at a lower unit cost than comparable North
West schemes, while avoiding significantly higher costs associated
with nightly?paid temporary accommodation.
 
Approving a two?year extension will allow the Council to avoid
the financial and market risks of re?procuring at a point when
provider capacity is noted as limited and support costs are rising.
The proposed uplift reflects inflationary pressures and supports
additional management capacity to reduce safeguarding and
operational risks linked to increasing client complexity. Not
opting to extend the contract would expose the Council to higher
accommodation costs. The proposed extension is therefore a
time?limited and cost?effective solution, to allow further work
during the extension period to assess longer?term need and
commissioning options.
 
The
proposed contract extension results in total expenditure of
£112,094 in 2026/27, £143,488 in 2027/28, and
£98,528 in 2028/29 (covering the period 1 April to 30
November 2028), compared with an original approved revenue budget
of £94,888 per annum. This results in a total additional
budget pressure across the 3 financial years of £69,445.
However, the scheme benefits from £51,772 per annum of legacy
Supporting People revenue funding to offset the contractual
expenditure. Any budget shortfall for 2028/29 beyond the November
contract end date, will need to be addressed through the
Council’s medium?term financial planning, alongside
consideration of any additional costs that may arise from future
re?procurement.
 
The
contract extension will be funded from approved Housing and
Homelessness revenue budgets for 2026/27 to 2027/28, supported by a
balance of legacy Supporting People funding allocated to Abbott
Lodge as part of the original Lot 3 procurement
exercise.
 
Legal advice obtained: Kathryn Saldanha, Commercial Legal Team,

The
Council’s Contract for Services with the Salvation Army in
respect of Abbott Lodge (the Abbott Lodge Contract) was awarded
following an open tender process which complied with the provisions
of the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR 2015) as well as the
Council’s own Contractual Standing Orders.
 
The
Abbott Lodge Contract was for an initial five-year term, with an
option for the Council to extend the Abbott Lodge Contract for a
further two years from 01/12/2026 to 30/11/2028.
 
As
set out at paragraph 4.0 of the report, Abbott Lodge is an
established supported housing scheme which provides wraparound 24
hour support for those with a high level of complex needs. The
Abbott Lodge supported housing scheme has been meeting the needs of
the Council successfully for several years and the Salvation Army
has established themselves as a valued delivery partner. The
Council therefore wishes to exercise its option to extend the
Abbott Lodge Contract until 30/11/2028.
 
As
set out at paragraph 4.0 of the report the Salvation Army cannot
continue to deliver the Abbott Lodge Contract at the original
agreed price whilst maintaining a longer-term viable scheme. The
original approved revenue budget for the Abbott Lodge Contract was
£94,888 per annum. As set out in the Financial Implications
below, the Council is seeking approval for the following increases
to the original approved revenue budget:
 

·     
Total Expenditure of £112,094 in 2026/27,
£143,488 in 2027/28, and £98,528 in 2028/29 (covering
the period 1 April to 30 November 2028).
 
This
means that there will be an increase in the total price of the
Abbott Lodge Contract of £69,445 across these 3 financial
years.
 
As
set out at paragraph 4.0 of the report, at the time the Abbott
Lodge Contract was procured there was no requirement for social
value targets. The Council has since worked with the Salvation Army
to identify a range of social value Themes, Outcomes & Measures
(TOMS) for the proposed contract extension period which will be
monitored and recorded by the Council through formal contract
meetings with the Salvation Army, rather than through The Social
Value Portal.
 
Regulation 72 of the PCR 2015 sets out the circumstances in
which contracts may be modified without a new procurement
procedure. In the case of the increase in the total price of the
Abbott Lodge Contract of £69,445 to cover the increased costs
of meeting the changing nature of client’s needs, the
conditions set out at Regulation 72(1)(c) of the PCR 2015 appear to
be met.

I Paul Dennett, City Mayor, in exercise of the powers contained
within the City Council Constitution do hereby:
 

Note the
transition to the Crisis Resilience Fund from 1 April 2026,
replacing the previous Household Support Fund and Discretionary
Housing Payment, and that Salford will receive ~£6m in each
of the next three years.

 

Note that Cabinet
previously endorsed initial allocations for 2026/27, under
authority included in the Council’s annual budget report to
Full Council in February 2026.

 

Agree to continue
with the current provision of holiday food support at £15pw
per eligible child, to support children and families in the city
with the cost of food during school holidays, for the remaining
four weeks (October, December and February) of 2026/27 school
holidays.

 

Note that options
setting out the proposed longer term use of the Crisis Resilience
Fund monies for 2027/28 and 2028/29 will be brought to Cabinet
later in the year, and in time to inform discussions as part of the
Council’s budget strategy and Medium Term Financial Plan for
February 2027.

 
The Reasons are:
 
Salford has for the
past few years used previous Household Support Fund monies to
support Holiday Vouchers for those families that are eligible for
free school meals.  This has represented
a significant commitment to families across the city and has
supported the priority to be a Child Friendly Salford.
 
Salford currently
spends around 50% of its CRF allocation supporting Holiday Voucher
provision. The CRF guidance states that authorities should use
their discretion to prioritise funding efficiently within their
own CRF schemes, including when considering how best to
support families in crisis to ensure the poorest children do not go
hungry in the school holidays. Current guidance states ‘this
may or may not be through the blanket provision of vouchers to
those on free-school meals, as it is recognised that some Free
School Meal eligible families may not routinely need crisis support
during every school holiday. Authorities should consider how best
to support the poorest and most in need households’.
 
At the same time as
the move to CRF, the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act
2026 introduces the most significant changes to FSM eligibility
since the introduction of Universal Credit.  In moving to new FSM arrangements, Government
requires that all existing FSM claims are revalidated under the new
rules.  This is being led by the
Council’s Revenue and Benefits Service. 
 
Salford currently
has approximately 17,410 live FSM claims recorded, and 94 of 100
schools subscribe to the Council’s FSM administration
service.  Initial reviews suggest
approx. 70% of those reviewed to date will continue to be eligible
for targeted FSM, meaning their household income remains below
£7,400 pa.  Many existing awards
do also remain in payment solely due to transitional protection and
may not continue under new arrangements. 
 
According to Public
Health England 
Child Health Profiles child poverty rates remain a concern
– in Salford 22% of children aged under 16 live in poverty in
the city (for the financial year ending 2021), higher than both the
national and regional average.  
DWP statistics note that 26% of children in Salford were living in
absolute low income families in 2023/24.  And rates vary considerably across the city. This
highlights the continued need for support to families and
children.
 
The recommended
option – to continue with holiday food support at the
existing level of £15 per week, per eligible child, will
continue to provide essential support to families, whilst we
complete the require reassessments for FSM and develop an evidence
led longer term approach that is both affordable and continues to
support families with the additional cost of food during the school
holidays.  Continuation is the simplest
and easiest for families and schools, without additional
applications or bureaucracy.  It
provides certainty up to and including February
half-term.   The cost of this
extension will be approx. £1.045 m, depending on eligibility
and take-up.
 
The transition to
CRF and the rebalancing of that funding is an opportunity to review
we support residents in crisis as well as how we work together,
across the Council and with partners, to prevent or avoid those
crises in the first place.  A rapid
review is proposed to set a longer term and sustainable and
affordable approach to supporting residents.  This will include insight from lived experience of
residents.  This work will be led by the
Lead Member for Housing and Tackling Poverty, with input from both
the Lead Member for Children’s Services and Adult
Services.  A cross-organisation working
group led by the Executive Director Corporate Services will support
this review.  Proposals for
consideration will be brough to Cabinet before the end of 2026, and
to inform decisions to be included in the 2027/28 budget strategy
and medium term financial plan.
 
Options considered and
rejected were:
 
Alternative options
considered and rejected were:
 

To taper holiday
food support.  This option would mean a
reducing level of financial support to individual families
reflecting the shift in Free School Meal eligibility.  As a positive this option would give families time
to adjust, continue to support families at most risk of financial
stress, and provide time for communications and awareness of the
changes.  This option was rejected as it
would though delay rather than resolve issues of longer term
affordability, and introduce greater complexity for families and
schools, without providing any long term certainty.  The cost would remain at circa £810,000
pa.

 

To end all holiday
food support.  Families would be able to
access food support via the Crisis Support scheme, via foodbanks
and food clubs.  This options was
rejected as it would provide insufficient time for families to
adjust to the withdrawal of financial support.  Child poverty remains a significant challenge
within the city.  Withdrawal would be
inconsistent with the Council’s priorities to tackle poverty
and to become a Child Friendly City.

Risk: Medium

Legal Advice
obtained:  Surjit Tour, City Solicitor and Monitoring
Officer
 
The Council has
power to administer the Crisis Resilience Fund and to determine a
local scheme for the allocation of support, subject to the terms of
the grant, any accompanying conditions and the published guidance.
The guidance makes clear that the Fund is intended to provide
crisis support and build financial resilience, with appropriate
governance, assessment, reporting, audit and fraud controls.
 
Continued use of
funding for a broad, automatic holiday voucher scheme based solely
on free school meal status would therefore carry increasing legal
and compliance risk unless it can be clearly justified as meeting
the Fund’s stated objectives and grant conditions. The report
provides sufficient justification for use of the Fund for holiday
school vouchers.
 
The recommendations
in this report are legally therefore supportable provided Cabinet
has regard to the CRF guidance, the Council’s budget
framework and the evidence set out in the report, including the
changing legal and policy context for free school meals from
September 2026.
 
Any transitional
continuation or tapering of holiday food vouchers for the remainder
of 2026/27 has been framed as a short-term, time-limited mitigation
to support orderly transition and avoidance of sudden hardship.
This demonstrates that the Council has balanced compassion,
fairness, affordability and compliance with the national
framework.

obtained: Rachel Rosewell, Chief Finance Officer.

includes proposals for the Crisis Resilience Fund (CRF) of
c£6m provided for each of the three years 2026/27 to 2028/29,

I Paul Dennett, City Mayor, in
consultation with Cabinet, in exercise of the powers contained
within the City Council Constitution do hereby approve the
recommendations to:
 

•  Note and review the financial position at the end
of June 2026 (Quarter 1) and the forecast revenue outturn position
of a £6.660m overspend for
2026/27.

•  Approve a virement of £5.8m from Centrally
Held budgets to the Adults and Health Partnerships
Directorate.

•  Approve acceptance of the retrospective 2026/27
funding allocations of £2.145m for the Best Start Family Hubs
and Healthy Babies Programme and
£2.094m for the national SEND Reform Programme.
 
The Reasons are:
 
The 2026/27 Quarter 1 revenue budget
monitoring report provides Cabinet with an update on the
Council’s financial position at the end of June 2026,
including the forecast revenue outturn position and an update on
general balances.
 
The financial position at the end of
Quarter 1 is a £6.660m revenue overspend for 2026/27
inclusive of the planned application of £21.417m from
earmarked reserves. The forecast reflects significant service
pressures offset by underspends in Centrally Held/Other
budgets.
 
The report seeks approval of a
£5.8m virement from Centrally Held budgets to Adults and
Health Partnerships and approval to accept
the retrospective 2026/27 funding allocations of £2.145m for Best Start
Family Hubs and £2.094m for SEND Reform.
 
The report also highlights ongoing
financial risks, including demand-led pressures within social care
and housing, the Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block
overspend, savings delivery and the planned use of
reserves.

I Paul
Dennett, City Mayor, in exercise
of the powers contained within the City Council
Constitution do hereby
approve:
 

The development and submission of an
application for Nature Towns and Cities Foundation Accreditation to
enable Salford to achieve recognised Nature City status.

 

The review and refresh of the
council's Greenspace Strategy to ensure it reflects current
evidence, corporate priorities and the requirements of the Nature
Towns and Cities accreditation framework.

 

The programme of stakeholder and
public consultation required to inform the refreshed Greenspace
Strategy and accreditation submission.

 
The Reasons
are:
 
The council has
secured almost £1 million of external funding through the
Nature Towns and Cities (NTC) programme, delivered in partnership
with Manchester City Council, to strengthen strategic planning for
green and blue infrastructure, improve access to nature, increase
community involvement and develop a pipeline of investable
projects. Achieving Nature City accreditation is one of the agreed
outputs of the funded programme and demonstrates the council's
commitment to delivering healthier, greener and more
climate-resilient neighbourhoods.
 
The revised
strategy will provide an updated evidence base, strengthen
cross-directorate working, support future investment opportunities
and ensure the council continues to meet its ambitions for
biodiversity, climate resilience and reducing health inequalities.
Failure to deliver the accreditation could affect delivery of the
approved grant outputs and may expose the council to financial and
reputational risk
 
Options considered
and rejected were: 
The council has considered the following
options.
 
Option 1 –
Proceed with Nature Towns and Cities Accreditation and refresh the
Greenspace Strategy (Preferred)
 
This option
delivers the approved outputs of the Nature Towns and Cities grant,
updates the council's strategic approach to green and blue
infrastructure and provides an opportunity to strengthen
partnership working, community engagement and future investment
readiness.
 
Benefits include:

delivery of grant commitments;
improved strategic planning;
stronger evidence base;
enhanced investment readiness;
improved partnership working;
updated corporate policy;
greater alignment with climate,
biodiversity and health priorities.

 
Risks are
considered manageable through the governance arrangements
established for the programme.
 
Option 2 –
Refresh the Greenspace Strategy without seeking accreditation
 
This option would
update the council's strategic framework but would fail to deliver
one of the approved outputs within the Nature Towns and Cities
funding agreement.
 
While some
strategic benefits would still be achieved, opportunities
associated with independent accreditation, national recognition and
investment confidence would be reduced.
 
This option also
increases the risk of challenge from the funding body regarding
delivery of approved programme outputs.
 
Option 3 –
Maintain the existing Greenspace Strategy and do not proceed with
accreditation
 
This option would
require no additional programme activity beyond existing
commitments.
 
However, it
would:

fail to deliver
one of the agreed grant outputs;
leave the council
operating under an increasingly outdated strategy;
reduce
opportunities to secure future external investment;
weaken strategic
alignment with current environmental policy;
increase financial
and reputational risk.

This option is not
recommended.
 
a)   
Preferred option and rationale
 
Option 1 is the
preferred option.
 
It delivers the
commitments contained within the approved Nature Towns and Cities
funding agreement while strengthening the council's long-term
strategic approach to green and blue infrastructure.
 
The proposal
provides an opportunity to refresh the Greenspace Strategy using
current evidence, strengthen partnership working, improve community
participation and position the council to attract additional
investment for environmental improvements.
The proposal also
supports delivery of wider corporate priorities relating to climate
resilience, biodiversity recovery, health inequalities,
regeneration and neighbourhood improvement.
The benefits of

within this report.

distilleries, and wineries reduces transport emissions, similarly
some brands utilize renewable energy and regenerative
agriculture.

Salford City Council – Record of

I, Councillor Cusack, Lead
Member for Corporate Services and Chairman of the Procurement
Board, accept the recommendation of the Procurement Board and in
exercise of the powers contained within the Council Constitution do
hereby approve:
 
·    
to undertake a procurement exercise for a Management
Information System (that integrates with and operates alongside
recently procured corporate management systems) for Regulatory
Services, Vehicle Management Services, Waste Management Services
and the Customer Contact Centre, and
 
·    
delegate authority to officers, in consultation with
Procurement and Legal Services, to undertake the procurement in
accordance with the Council's Contract Procedure Rules and the
Procurement Act 2023, noting that the route to market will be
determined following the market engagement.
 
The Reasons are:
The Council's existing Civica
APP Management Information System is a legacy product which is no
longer being actively developed and the current contract expires on
31 March 2028. A procurement exercise is therefore required to
secure a modern replacement solution, support service resilience
and ensure continuity of service delivery across Regulatory
Services, Vehicle Management Services, Waste Management Services
and the Customer Contact Centre.
 
Options considered and rejected
were:
·    
Do nothing. This option was rejected as it would
increase the risk of service disruption and leave the Council
without a suitable Management Information System when the current
contract expires.
 
·    
Extend the use of the current system. This option
was rejected as the system is a legacy product which is no longer
actively developed and no longer fully meets service
requirements.
 
Procuring a replacement system
is the preferred option and is recommended.
 
Assessment of Risk:
The principal risk is failure
to secure and implement a replacement Management Information System
before expiry of the current contract. This could adversely impact
case management, workflow management, customer interactions,
reporting and operational service delivery across several council
services. The proposed procurement exercise mitigates this risk by
allowing time for procurement, implementation, testing, training
and migration activities prior to contract expiry.
 
Innovate/ Best Value –
identify the relevant corporate priorities specific to
Salford:
·    
Continuous improvement.
·    
Use of resources.
·    
Service delivery.
·    
Partnerships and community engagement.
 
The proposed procurement will
support the Council's commitment to Best Value by improving
efficiency, reducing manual processes and making greater use of
automation across service areas. The implementation of a new
Management Information System will enhance reporting capabilities,
improve the customer experience and provide opportunities to
consolidate existing systems, supporting more integrated ways of
working. Collectively, these improvements are expected to
contribute to more effective service delivery and better value for
money through the efficient use of resources.
 
The source of funding and
financial advice obtained:
Supplied by Paul Guest – Finance Manager –
07/08/2026
The current Civica APP contract
expires on 31 March 2028, and Civica have advised that APP is a
legacy product and is no longer being actively developed. As a
result, the Council is required to consider an alternative platform
to support its management information requirements.
 
The procurement process will
initially be market engagement through supplier workshops to better
understand current market capabilities, emerging technologies,
implementation approaches, indicative costs and available
procurement routes.
 
The council currently has
budget provision of £80,000 per annum for the existing Civica
APP licence, maintenance and support arrangements. Initial market
intelligence indicates that the cost of a replacement solution
could be in excess of £350,000 over a five year period,
although costs remain subject to market engagement and
competition.
 
In addition to on-going licence
and supports costs, there are likely to be one off implementation,
migration, configuration and training costs. These costs are not
yet known and will be refined through the procurement process. Any
additional funding requirements will be considered through the
Medium Term Financial Plan and future approval reports seeking
authority to award the contract.
 
Legal Advice
obtained:
Supplied by Lauren Armstrong
– Commercial Legal – 29/07/2026
This report seeks approval to
undertake a competitive market exercise to procure an MIS system as
described above. When purchasing goods or commissioning services,
the Council must comply with its own internal Contractual Standing
Orders, and the relevant Procurement legislation (being either
Procurement Act 2023, or Public Contracts Regulations 2015 if
utilising a framework let before the new regime came into
force).
 
Legal is happy to support
officers with this process. If the Council is designing and
undertaking its own process then Legal can assist with putting
together the draft form of contract to be included in the tender
pack for bidders to value and submit their bids against.
Alternatively the Council may utilise an existing framework such as
G-Cloud, which already has its own form of Call-Off contract. If
using a pre-existing framework the Council will need to comply with
the call-off requirements.
 
If the existing and/or incoming
system/services either stores or processes individual’s
personal data (particularly sensitive or special category data)
then the Council’s Information Governance team will need to
provide support to ensure that compliance with the Data Protection
Act 2018 (for example a data protection impact assessment may be
required, updates to existing Council privacy notices etc once a
provider is identified).
 
Procurement Advice
obtained:
Supplied by Jayne Whitehead – Interim Category Procurement
Manager – 16/07/2026
Procurement will advise on the
best route to market following market engagement in line with the
Councils constitution and Public Contract Regulations PA23. Where a
framework is available to meet the service needs these will be
reviewed before a decision is made to run an open market
tender.
 
The Council reserves the right
not to proceed with any procurement process and potentially may
consider direct award or further competition under a relevant
framework as a route to market.
 
The procurement will include
Social Value requirements aligned to the Council's Social Value
Framework. Suppliers will be required to demonstrate how they will
deliver social, economic and environmental benefits, including
employment and apprenticeship opportunities, local supply chain
participation, skills development and carbon reduction
initiatives.
 
HR Advice obtained:
Supplied by Rachel Rennie - HR&OD Business Partner –
29/07/2026
There are no direct HR
implications at this stage. In the future when a management
information system has been selected, the Service will need to
ensure the workforce are communicated with, engaged and appropriate
training arrangements are offered to support the implementation of
any new system.
 
Climate Change Implications
obtained:
Supplied by Hayley Nixon – Strategic Lead Net Zero –
30/07/2026
The GM 5 Year
Environment Plan commits GM and Salford City Council to carbon
neutrality by 2038.
 
This system will
support the Council's commitment by enabling more efficient and
digital service delivery. Benefits include reduced paper use, less
physical storage, and reduced officer travel through mobile
working.

·

compliant framework or Dynamic Purchasing System, including a

commissioning and maintenance of up to four Solar EV Charging Hubs
at council-owned sites, with an estimated contract value of
£846,808 funded through CRSTS and Invest to Save
funding.
 
The
Reasons are:
To enable
the delivery of the Solar EV Charging Hub Pilot, maximise the use
of the remaining CRSTS Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure
allocation, secure best value through a compliant procurement
process, and support the Council's climate change, decarbonisation
and sustainable transport objectives.
 
Options
considered and rejected were:
Alternative options for utilising the remaining CRSTS allocation
were considered, including other forms of EV charging
infrastructure. Solar EV Charging Hubs were identified as the
preferred intervention because they combine renewable energy
generation with EV charging infrastructure, can reduce reliance on
grid upgrades, provide publicly accessible charging facilities and
generate evidence to inform future investment decisions.
 
Key
decision: YES.
 
Assessment of Risk:
Medium.
Risks include procurement delays, site-specific constraints,
supplier availability, technology performance and lower than
expected utilisation. These risks will be managed through robust
procurement, project governance, site assessments, stakeholder
engagement and contract management arrangements.
 
Innovate/
Best Value – identify the relevant corporate priorities
specific to Salford:

The Solar EV Charging Hub Pilot represents an
innovative approach to delivering Electric Vehicle Charging
Infrastructure by combining solar photovoltaic generation and EV
charging facilities within a single modular solution. The project
will test an emerging technology that has the potential to reduce
reliance on grid upgrades, minimise installation timescales and
improve the efficiency of infrastructure delivery compared to more
traditional charging solutions.

 

The proposed procurement will ensure that the
Council secures best value through a competitive process, enabling
the market to demonstrate how it can meet the Council’s
requirements while delivering value for money, quality and social
value outcomes. The project will also provide valuable operational
and commercial data to inform future investment decisions, business
cases and the potential wider deployment of Solar EV Charging Hubs
across the city.

 

The pilot supports the Council’s commitment to
innovation by trialling new approaches to EV charging provision,
renewable energy generation and integrated mobility solutions. It
will help establish an evidence base for future investment and
contribute towards the Council’s climate change, sustainable
transport and carbon reduction objectives.
 
The
source of funding and financial advice obtained:
£446,808 from the City Region Sustainable Transport
Settlement (CRSTS) Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure
allocation and up to £400,000 from Invest To Save funding
within the Low Carbon Capital Programme 2026/27.
 
Legal
Advice obtained: Supplied by:
Daniel Howard, Principal Lawyer, Legal Services – 0161 600
8733 / date: 29 July 2026
When commissioning contracts for the procurement of
goods, services, or the execution of works the Council must comply
with the applicable procurement legislation as well as its own
Contractual Standing Orders (CSO’s), Financial Regulations
and the duties of Best and Social value. In addition, the Act
requires that contracting authorities treat candidates equally and
in a non-discriminatory way and act in a transparent manner,
failing which the award of a contract may be subject to legal
challenge.
 
The report sets out that the Council proposes to
undertake a procurement process via either an existing compliant
Framework Agreement or Dynamic Purchasing System. Using a compliant
framework or dynamic purchasing system will give some comfort to
the Council in ensuring that value for money is being obtained and
periodically tested, with competition maintained. The carrying out
of this procurement exercise in accordance with the terms of the
applicable framework or DPS will ensure that the risk of challenge
to the award of the contract to the selected contractor is minimal
and that any challenge, should it materialise, is unlikely to be
successful.
 
Procurement Advice obtained: Supplied by
Daniel Cunliffe, Category Manager, 0161 686 6249
The
procurement activity will use a suitable framework to source this
work. A number of DPS agreements by different contracting
authorities that we can utilise, we are reviewing the options that
are best suited for SCC. The DPS process is in line with the
Procurement Act 2023/Public Contract Regulations 2015 and SCC
governance procedures.
 
Financial
advice obtained: Supplied by: Ian
Cowburn, Senior Accountant
Date provided: 30/07/2026 – Expenditure Code:
A10310/D07188
a) Source of Funding:
i. CRSTS: GMCA has allocated £7.55M of CRSTS
funding across the 10 GM authorities as part of the Electric
Vehicle Charging Infrastructure initiative. Salford’s
allocation is £708,208, of which £146,000 has already
been drawn down, leaving £562,208 funding available.
£446,808 of this will be used as a contribution to the cost
of the proposed solar hubs.
ii. Invest to Save: The £400,000 balance of the
proposed contract will come from Invest To Save funding within the
Low Carbon Capital Programme 2026/27.
 
b) Financial Implications:
This is a request for approval to go out to tender
for the delivery of four solar EV charging hubs. This will be
funded in part by CRSTS grant provided to us from the DfT via GMCA,
with the remainder coming from Invest To Save funding within the
Low Carbon Capital Programme 2026/27.
 
The CRSTS grant is subject to GMCA approval of
SCC’s Strategic Outline Business Case, the procurement
process is required for the Business Case. There is a potential
financial risk associated with the CRSTS grant as the grant
conditions require that funds are committed by March
2027.
 
The solar hubs are expected to generate income from
their use by the public, it is also anticipated that the hubs will
provide a cheaper source of electricity for council-owned
vehicles.
 
HR Advice
obtained: N/A.
 
Climate
Change Implications obtained:
The GM 5
Year Environment Plan commits GM to increasing local renewable
energy generation by at least 375MW by 2030 and increasing the
uptake of active travel and Electric Vehicles solutions.
 
This
pilot project represents an innovative approach that could be
scaled and adopted by SCC and other authorities. SCC already has a
substantial portfolio of renewable generation assets, and this
project aims to vary the type and usage of renewable
generation.
 
While one of the primary
drivers for this pilot is the increased use of EV charging there is
the potential for income, reduced electricity costs and the project
reduce SCC’s carbon emissions.This
approach will enhance energy resilience, improve financial
efficiency, and contribute to the Council’s broader carbon
neutrality.

Salford City Council
- Record of Decision (Cabinet)
 
I, Tracey
Kelly, Statutory Deputy City Mayor, in exercise of the powers
contained within the City Council Constitution do hereby approve:
 
The
designation of an additional licensing scheme for Section 257
Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), under Part 2 of the Housing
Act 2004 in Salford having regard to the evidence base contained
within consultation document, the consultation responses contained
within Appendix B, the legislative requirements and non-statutory
guidance.
 
The proposed fee structure for the additional
licensing scheme Section 257 Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs)
as detailed in Appendix D;
 
The proposed Licence Conditions for the
additional licensing scheme for Section 257   Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) as
detailed Annex 1 of Appendix A – the consultation
document;
 
Authorises officers to carry out all necessary
actions to publicise the designation for additional licensing
scheme for Section 257 Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) to
comply with the requirements of the Housing Act 2004.
 
Acknowledges that the scheme is self-funding
and staffing resources to deliver the scheme will be approved under
delegated powers by the Deputy Chief Executive (Executive Director
of Place)
 
The Reasons
are:
Having considered all of the available
evidence and the representations made in accordance with the public
consultation (and not withdrawn) I am satisfied a significant
proportion of Section 257 HMOs across the city are being managed
sufficiently ineffectively as to give rise, or to be likely to give
rise, to one or more particular problems either for those occupying
the HMOs or for members of the public; and that making a
designation will, when combined with other measures taken in the
area by the local housing authority, or by persons together with
the local housing authority, contribute to the improvement of the
social or economic conditions in the area.
 
I have considered whether there are any other
courses of action available to the local housing authority that
might provide an effective method of achieving the objective that
the designation would be intended to achieve and consider that
making the designation will significantly assist the local housing
authority to achieve the objectives (whether or not they take any
other course of action as well). It is considered that the scheme
will complement the wider regeneration that Salford City Council is
helping to deliver.  Additional HMO
licensing will address existing issues of poor property and tenancy
management in privately rented accommodation.  The scheme will also ensure that new landlords
investing in the Salford understand what is expected of them and
will sustain the strong community that the regeneration programmes
have worked hard to establish.
 
Options considered and rejected were:

·      
Take no action – this would be inconsistent with established
Council policy and would fail to address the legitimate concerns of
residents, local elected members and other stakeholders regarding
the impact of the private rented sector on the local housing
market.
·      
Defer the introduction of additional HMO licensing in Salford
– A review of current policy and available evidence suggests
that a significant proportion of Section 257 HMOs across the city
are being managed sufficiently ineffectively as to give rise, or to
be likely to give rise, to one or more particular problems either
for those occupying the HMOs or for members of the public.
 
Assessment of Risk: The risk is considered low.
 
Salford City Council considers that it has
made a robust and well?evidenced case for the designation of a
Selective Licensing Scheme.
 
The formal consultation ran for the full
10?week period and was supported by a range of awareness?raising
activity, including social media campaigns, direct engagement with
stakeholders, and the distribution of leaflets in community centres
and gateway locations. Of those reached, 206 individuals clicked
through to view the consultation, and 51 went on to complete it.
This indicates that while awareness of the consultation was
advertised only small proportion of people  were actively interest in learning more and chose
to engage in detail with the proposals.
 
The majority of landlords and managing agents
who responded to the consultation did not support the proposal.
Their views have been carefully considered. However, the responses
did not present a substantive challenge to the evidence base set
out in the consultation document, nor did they include alternative
data, practical evidence, or constructive counter?proposals to
support the opinions expressed. As a result, the weight that can
reasonably be attached to those responses is limited.
 
Salford City Council recognises that any
decision made in relation to this proposal may be subject to legal
challenge. For this reason, careful consideration has been given to
the consultation process, the evidence base, and all
representations received statutory guidance and formal process, to
ensure that any decision taken is lawful, proportionate and
evidence?led.
 
The source of funding is: Landlord Licensing is a self-financing scheme over
its five-year life. If implemented in this area the costs for
running the scheme will be recovered through revenue acquired from
the licence fee chargeable to landlords. 
 
Legal Advice
obtained:
 
Part 2 of the Housing Act 2004 makes
provision for the designation of areas
subject to additional licensing.
 
In that regard, a local housing authority may
designate either–
 
(a)  the area of their district,
or
(b)  an area in their district,
 
as subject to additional licensing in relation
to a description of HMOs specified in
the designation, if the requirements of
section 56 are met.
 
The authority must consider that a significant
proportion of the HMOs of that
description in the area are being managed
sufficiently ineffectively as to give rise,
or to be likely to give rise, to one or more
particular problems either for those
occupying the HMOs or for members of the
public.
 
Before making a designation, the authority
must–
 
(a)  take reasonable steps to
consult persons who are likely to be affected by the designation;
and
(b)  consider any representations
made in accordance with the consultation and not withdrawn.
 
The power to make a designation under this
section may be exercised in such a
way that this Part applies to all HMOs in the
area in question.
 
In forming an opinion as to the matter
mentioned in subsection (2), the authority
must have regard to any information regarding
the extent to which any codes of
practice approved under section
233 have been complied with by persons
managing HMOs in the area in question.
 

Section 57 of the Housing Act 2004 also applies in respect of
additional licensing
schemes. In that regard, the authority must
ensure that any exercise of the power
is consistent with the authority's overall
housing strategy.
 
The authority must also seek to adopt a
co-ordinated approach in connection with
dealing with homelessness, empty properties
and anti-social behaviour affecting
the private rented sector, both–
 
(a)  as regards combining licensing
under this Part with other courses of action available to them,
and
(b)  as regards combining such
licensing with measures taken by other persons.
 
The authority must not make a particular
designation under section 56 of the Act
unless–
 
(a)  they have considered whether
there are any other courses of action available to them (of
whatever nature) that might provide an effective method of dealing
with the problem or problems in question, and
(b)  they consider that making the
designation will significantly assist them to deal with the problem
or problems (whether they take any other course of action as
well).
 
The report updates decision makers regarding
the outcome of the recent consultation exercise undertaken under
section 56 of the Housing Act 2004 and makes a number of
recommendations accordingly. 
 
When exercising public functions, the Council
must ensure that it complies with the public sector equality duty
as set out in section 149 of the Equality Act 2010. In that regard,
an impact assessment measures and records compliance with this
duty
 
Financial Advice obtained: This report
seeks approval to designate a citywide Additional HMO licensing
scheme for Section 257 Houses in Multiple Occupation in Salford,
for a five-year period.

I, Tracey Kelly, Statutory Deputy City Mayor, in
exercise of the powers contained within the City Council
Constitution do hereby approve:
 
The proposed
Planned Carriageway Patching Programme for 2026/27 funded through
the Department for Transport Local Highway Maintenance Fund
allocation of £1.401 million.
 
The Reasons are:
 
To facilitate
delivery of an evidence-led programme of planned carriageway
patching works, improving highway condition, reducing the rate of
asset deterioration and supporting a whole-life asset management
approach to highway maintenance. The programme will also support
compliance with Department for Transport Local Highway Maintenance
Fund transparency requirements.
 
Options considered
and rejected were: No other
options were considered for this report.
 
Final Decision:

Approval is granted
for the Planned Carriageway Patching Programme for 2026/27 as
outlined in the report. The programme will utilise the confirmed
Department for Transport Local Highway Maintenance Fund allocation
of £1.401 million to deliver planned carriageway patching
works across the highway network using a combination of in-house
operational teams and framework contractors.


 
Assessment of Risk:

Low. The targeted
use of available funding will support the Council in meeting its
statutory duties under the Highways Act 1980 whilst improving the
condition and resilience of the highway network. By intervening at
the optimal point in the asset lifecycle, the programme aims to
reduce future deterioration, minimise the need for more costly
reconstruction works and improve overall value for money.


Source of Funding:
Department for Transport Local Highway Maintenance Fund allocation
of £1.401 million for 2026/27 received via Transport
for Greater Manchester.


Legal Advice Obtained:
In relation to the Highways Act 1980 the requirement to maintain
pot holes will fall under the Council’s general duty as
Highway Authority to maintain highways maintainable at public
expense.
 
Section 58 of the
Highways Act 1980 provides a statutory defence to the Section 41
duty in an action against the Highway Authority for having failed
in its duty to maintain a highway within its control. Section 58
states that it is a defence (without prejudice to any other defence
or the application of the law relating to contributory negligence)
to such action if the authority had taken such care as in all the
circumstances was reasonably required to secure that the part of
the highway to which the action relates was not dangerous for
traffic.
 
Section 58 lists
the matters a Court will have regard to in relation to the defence.
This includes such matters as the character of the highway,
appropriate standard of maintenance, expected state of repair and
traffic expected to use it. It also includes:
 
1. whether the
highway authority knew, or could reasonably have been expected to
know, that the condition of the part of the highway to which the
action relates was likely to cause danger to users of the highway;
and
 
2. where the
highway authority could not reasonably have been expected to repair
that part of the highway before the cause of action arose, what
warning notices of its condition had been displayed;
 
Therefore, provided
the Council is satisfied that it has carried out a full and
thorough scope of repairs needed across the Highway
Authority’s area to repair pot holes and what other remedial
measures are in place to protect the public in the meantime, the
risk to the Council arising out of any litigation should be
minimal.
Supplied by: Helen
Chapman, Principal Solicitor


Procurement Advice Obtained:
The planned patching programme will be delivered through in-house
teams and also external contractors within the council’s own
Technical and Highways Works Framework as required.  This is complaint with SCC standing orders and
PCR’s 2015.
Supplied by: Heather Stanton, Category
Manager


Financial Advice Obtained:
This report sets out details of the Carriageway Patching Programme
to be financed by DfT Additional Highways Maintenance funding of
£1.401M awarded to SCC via GMCA in 2026-27.
 
The funding of £1.401M was received from
GMCA on 17 April 2026 so it is available for use on the Patching
Programme.
DfT has indicated that a proportion of the
Additional Highways Maintenance funding is linked to submission of
a Local Highways Maintenance Transparency Report. SCC met this
requirement in 2025-26 and intends to again comply with this
requirement in 2026-27 to ensure that there is no loss of Highways
Maintenance Funding in future.
Supplied by: Ian Cowburn, Senior
Accountant


Equality Impact Assessment:
The programme will have a positive impact on all equality groups by
improving accessibility and safety for pedestrians, including the
elderly and those with mobility impairments. Works will include
tactile paving and dropped kerbs at junctions.


Climate Change Implications:
None identified.

All.

robust and compliant with the requirements of the Council’s

I Paul Dennett, City Mayor, in exercise of the powers contained within the City

The ten-year
(2026-2036) Library Strategy for Salford, together with a
commitment that a detailed Library Service Delivery Plan will be
developed and presented for approval within 12 months of adoption
of the Strategy.

 
The Delivery Plan
will set out clear priorities, aligned to the seven objectives
stated within the Strategy, in addition to key milestones, resource
requirements, delivery timescales, measurable outcomes and
performance indicators to support implementation of the
Strategy.
 
The Reasons are:
 
The Library
Strategy (2026-2036) provides Salford with its first long-term
strategic framework for the development of a modern, inclusive and
sustainable library service. Establishing a clear vision to guide
the service over the next decade: “Libraries at the heart
of Salford - connecting communities and empowering learning,
creativity and wellbeing”, the strategy recognises the
vital role libraries play in supporting residents and communities
across the city.
 
Developed through
extensive research, analysis and stakeholder engagement, the
strategy will ensure that the Library Service is well placed to
respond to changing demographic, social and economic needs. The
Strategy is underpinned by seven strategic objectives focused on
community hubs, children and young people, literacy, arts and
culture, digital inclusion, lifelong learning and employment, and
partnership working and sustainability. Together, these objectives
provide a clear framework, enabling libraries to play a full role
in delivering the Council's wider ambitions and addressing key
city-wide challenges such as inequalities, low literacy levels,
digital exclusion and health inequalities.

I Paul Dennett, the City Mayor, in consultation with
Cabinet in exercise of the powers contained within the City Council
Constitution do hereby approve the publication of the Community
Safety Partnership Domestic Abuse and Intimate Partner
Sexual Violence Strategy 2026–2031
 
The Reasons are:
 
The Salford
Domestic Abuse and Intimate Partner Sexual Violence Strategy
2026–2031 (the Strategy) is a five?year multi-agency
partnership strategy to prevent domestic abuse, support victims and
survivors, hold perpetrators to account, and strengthen
multi?agency working across the City of Salford. 
The Strategy aligns
with the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 and key national, regional and
local drivers. Preventing domestic abuse and supporting residents
who are victims and survivors of domestic abuse is a core priority
for Salford City Council (the Council). 
It is important that those who experience domestic abuse can get
the support they need and that agencies work together to safeguard
victims.
 
This is an
ambitious Strategy recognising the scale of the issue within
Salford – in 2024/25 domestic abuse accounted for 17% of all
committed crimes recorded by GMP in Salford and our commissioned
domestic abuse service received 3330 referrals. 44% of cases heard
at the high-risk Multi-agency Risk Assessment Conference had
children in the household and 95% of Bridge Referrals had domestic
abuse related incidents.
 
Extensive
consultation took place to develop the Strategy that involved a
wide range of stakeholders, a public consultation, the VCSE sector
and gaining the views of people with lived experience of domestic
abuse.
The Strategy,
through it’s approach to perpetrators and those who cause
harm, whilst absolutely recognising the criminal justice response
is essential, also advocates for supporting behaviour change in
people who cause harm. Programmes commissioned to work with
perpetrators of domestic abuse and our approach to these align with
this principle and are evidence-based behaviour change
programmes.
 
Options considered and
rejected were: 
 
The option to do
nothing was rejected because it would leave Salford without an
up-to-date strategic framework for addressing domestic abuse and
intimate partner sexual violence. This would weaken the
partnership's ability to coordinate activity, respond to emerging
needs, and deliver on local and national priorities. Failure to
publish the Strategy could reduce accountability, limit
opportunities to improve outcomes for victims and survivors, and
undermine the Council’s and partners’ commitment to
preventing abuse and creating safer communities.
 
Assessment of
Risk: Low
The risk associated
with publishing the Community Safety Partnership Domestic Abuse and
Intimate Partner Sexual Violence Strategy 2026–2031 is
assessed as low because it sets out a co-ordinated framework for
partnership working, building on established priorities, evidence,
and legislative requirements. Publication supports transparency,
accountability and public awareness of the Council's and partners'
commitments to tackling domestic abuse and sexual violence.
Appropriate governance, consultation and information assurance
processes have been followed during its development, minimising
operational, legal and reputational risks. Any potential risks are
outweighed by the benefits of providing a clear strategic direction
for improving outcomes for victims, survivors and communities
across Salford.
 
The source of funding
is:
 
Not applicable for
the Strategy as the strategy has been developed through officer
time.
 
Legal Advice
obtained:
 
Under the legislationthe Council must
produce a strategy setting outhow it intends
to comply with its duty under Part IV of the Domestic Abuse Act
2021 to provide support to victims of domestic abuse and their
children when they are in safe accommodation.  The
Strategy set out in thisdocument supports this work and recognises
delivery of the Domestic Abuse Support in Safe Accommodation
Strategy as a key priority.
 
Barbara Gora
 
Financial Advice
obtained:
 
Karen Wilcha, Senior Accountant
Dated : 26/05/2026
 
The
Strategy is a comprehensive and well-articulated document, setting
out a strong, partnership-led approach to tackling domestic abuse
and intimate partner sexual violence across Salford.  It demonstrates clear alignment with the Domestic
Abuse Act 2021 and wider strategic priorities, ensuring the
approach reflects current legislative and policy
expectations.
 
The
Strategy is supported by funding through the Domestic Abuse Grant,
which contributes to the provision of commissioned services for
victims and their families, including those in safe
accommodation.  Delivery is further
strengthened through collaboration with the Domestic Abuse Housing
Advisory core group.  This approach is
informed by ongoing service reviews, needs assessments, and is
subject to the availability and allocation of grant
funding.

is implemented.

across Salford.

The Reasons:
for the decision and report is to extend the framework contract,
allowing continuity of delivery of works to be commissioned and
undertaken by suitably appointed contractors within the framework.
An exception to award an extension is being sought.
 
Options considered and
rejected were:
Salford is in the final year of a 4 year framework
and requires additional time to ensure a compliant and fit for
purpose new framework is in place going forward. Alternative
frameworks are available including the Bolton and Manchester
Framework; however, the availability of contractors who are already
commissioned by other GM authorities cannot guarantee their
commitment to deliver the scale of works required to be delivered
during the extension period and the working relationships have not
been established. Hence, this was the preferred procurement route. Work cannot be
undertaken in-house as there are insufficient resources.
 
Assessment of
Risk:
If the extension to the framework is not approved
Salford will not be able to deliver planned and agreed programmes
of work already agreed as part of the budget approval process for
26/27. There will therefore be slippage in budget spend this
current financial year.
 
This risk will likely
then extend into next financial year 27/28 and future schemes and
programmes yet to be agreed for next financial year will not be
able to be fully delivered having a likely knock on effect into
further years.
 
There is a risk that
we would not be able to deliver schemes and works that are grant
funded with specific deadlines for delivery e.g. GMCA/ TfGM.
Salford could in effect lose current funding and the lack of spend
could risk securing expected or funding from future settlements due
to non-delivery of commitments already given.
 
Some works are also required to
be undertaken to ensure that the council meets its statutory duties
with regard to maintaining highway assets and hence could be
subject to increased insurance liability.
 
The source of
funding: is a mixture of approved capital and revenue funding
depending on the nature of work being undertaken.
 
Legal Advice
obtained:Ordinarily when
commissioning contracts for the procurement of goods, services or
the execution of works the Council as a ‘contracting
authority’ must comply with public procurement legislation as
well as the provisions of its own Contractual Standing Orders
(CSO’s), Financial Regulations and the duties of Best and
Social value. In addition, the Public Contracts Regulations 2015
(which were in force when the framework was set up) require that
contracting authorities treat candidates equally and in a
non-discriminatory way and act in a transparent manner, failing
which the award of a contract may be subject to legal
challenge.
 
In that regard, the Framework
Agreement was set up following a compliant tender process in
accordance with legislation in force at the time and CSO’s by
way of the opportunity for the existing framework being
appropriately advertised as an open competition inviting interested
companies to submit bids to be appointed to the relevant lot(s) for
a period of four years. That period is almost at expiry, and the
report sets out the reasons and exceptional circumstances for the
Council to dispense with strict compliance of its CSO’s.
Nonetheless, there is still a risk of challenge from aggrieved
providers if the usual tender process has not been followed on the
basis that the opportunity ought to have been advertised and put
out to competition.
 
Whilst generally speaking the
4-year term for a framework can't be exceeded, there's a "save in
exceptional circumstances" carve out in the Public Contracts
Regulations 2015 (“PCR”) although that's really
intended for when setting the framework up in first place, so the
4-year period isn't an absolute that can't be exceeded. Any
provision for extension, or for a longer term than the 4-year
period would usually be done either at the start of setting up the
framework, or at least during its term.
 
The value of each individual
contract let would be under the statutory works contracts threshold
(£5,193,000), so if there were any challenge/complaint
regarding an individual contract the Council could validate that by
doing a separate exception report for those works if needs
be.
 
Going forward, during the
extension period, when awarding contracts, the only issue might be
whether any funding for a particular job has come from third party
grant funding with specific requirements to comply with public
procurement rules, as the Council would want to avoid potential
claims of clawback of the grant for failing to strictly
comply.
 
As a final point, it's a
relatively short-term extension anyway which mitigates the risk of
challenge or complaint, and in these circumstances, contractors
will generally be more concerned with bidding for the new framework
which is imminent.
 
As the potential value of the
framework exceeds £1 million, approval for the award should
be made be by the City Mayor acting on the recommendation of the
Procurement Board.
 
Financial Advice
obtained:
There are no direct financial implications to be
considered as contracts let under these frameworks will be
considered/reported on a scheme by scheme basis.
 
Procurement Advice

arrived whereby a further extension is required to complete the
work required for the new Technical Framework to go out to market.
The new framework will comply with the Procurement Act 2023 and is
anticipated to be for a total of 8 years.

proposed Salford Crescent to MediaCityUK – Bus Stop
Upgrades.
·     
endorse the proposed procurement route for the
scheme, via an existing framework in accordance with the
Council’s Contract Procurement Rules.  
 
The Reasons are:
The bus stop improvements
proposed as part of this package of works, will improve access to
and the integration of sustainable travel modes for the residents
of Salford and beyond. And help support the regions target of being
carbon neutral by 2038.
 
Options considered and rejected
were: None.
 
Assessment of Risk:
Medium.
The process of setting budgets
for the CRSTS funding settlement which took place several years
ago, means that inflationary pressures in the construction sector
have increased substantially since the funding allocations were bid
for and agreed.
 
The government funding letter
to Greater Manchester confirms ‘Any cost overruns must be met
locally and no additional HMG (Government) funding from this
settlement will be provided to support your CRSTS
programmes’.
 
This means that the work funded
by the programme may have to be reduced in scope as inflation
pressures continue to erode what can be delivered with the funding
allocated.
 
It will be important to develop
the interventions working in close collaboration with the Greater
Manchester and Active Travel England governance and approval
gateway processes, to ensure the risk of funding claw back is
minimised as projects progress beyond development to the delivery
phase of the project.
Securing funding for the SI
work at this stage, reduces the risk of insufficient

This agreement covers the delivery of Bikeability cycle training in

Bikeability cycle training is a
nationally central government funded scheme which teaches children
to ride safely on the highway and reinforces key road safety
messages which are vital in reducing casualties on the highway. The
scheme has been running for several years successfully in Salford
and is an integral part of road safety education in
schools.
 
The procurement sought agencies
that not only deliver quality service within the city but also
align with Salford’s commitment to social value, customer

extensive record of delivery throughout GM spanning over 20
years.

different levels of management within the service, ensuring a
balanced and informed assessment. All panel members have experience

from the first day of transfer, provision must be made for the

available for deployment ahead of the planned transfer date of 1

2)             
Grant approval for public consultation on the update
to the Local List to include updates to existing entries, removals
from the list and new additions.
 
The
Reasons are:
Following the updating of the
data held on Locally Listed assets.
 
Options considered and
rejected were: N/A
 
Assessment of Risk:
This report sets out the
approach that has been taken to comprehensively update the Local
List. This consultation will give the opportunity for local
residents and consultees to comment on the proposed changes and
these representations will be taken into account at the adoption
stage. The assessment of risk at this stage of the process is
therefore low. 
 
The
source of funding is:
The production of the documents

funding from the Council.
 
Legal Advice
obtained:
Justin Hobson, Principal Lawyer
Planning Practice Guidance
(PPG) encourages local planning authorities to identify
non-designated heritage assets (such as buildings, monuments,
sites, places, areas or landscapes) that have a degree of heritage
significance meriting consideration in planning decisions, but
which do not meet the criteria for designated heritage asset
status.  Such assets may be identified
by means of a Local List of Heritage Assets.  The identification and inclusion of non-designated
heritage assets on the Local List must be based on sound
evidence.
 
The National Planning Policy
Framework (NPPF) requires that the effect of a planning application
on the significance of a non-designated heritage asset (such as
those included on a Local List) should be taken into account in
determining the application.  In
weighing applications that directly or indirectly affect
non-designated heritage assets, a balanced judgement will be
required having regard to the scale of any harm or loss and the
significance of the heritage asset.
 
It should be noted that the
inclusion of a heritage asset on the Local List does not subject
the asset to statutory controls, such as those which relate to
listed building under the Planning (Listed Buildings and
Conservation Areas) Act 1990.

obtained: Ethan Bestwick /
Accountant

The update to
Salford’s Local List will help alleviate the impacts of
climate change. The conservation of Salford’s historic
environment via the list will encourage the retaining and reuse of
heritage assets; thus, circumventing material and energy costs
associated with new development.

for areas previously designated as Conservation Areas.
 
2)             
Grant approval to go out for public consultation on
the proposed boundary changes to the Conservation Areas whose
boundaries we are seeking to alter.
 
3)             
Grant approval to go out for public consultation on
the newly proposed designation of a Conservation Area at
Ordsall.
 
The

consultation and future adoption.

Assessment of Risk:
This report is to seek approval to
begin public consultation the draft Conservation Area Appraisals
and Management Plans. At that stage we will seek the opinions of
stakeholders, residents and consultees and take their views into
account prior to the adoption of any documents. This stage of the
process therefore the risk is low.
 
The
source of funding is:
